works_at.note: NOT MODELLED. His premises are located by his own advertisement to the east end of South Water Street and there is no structure record for them, so there is nothing to point at. The east end of South Water is the part of the street nearest the fort and the reservation, which is a district this dataset is thin in.

present_on_scene_date.note: Documented in the town in November 1833 and not followed by anything reached to 1835. A clothier and grocer at the east end of South Water in the year the harbour opened is more likely than not to have stayed, but 'more likely than not' is what the uncertain value is for.

persons.name: Peter Cohen

occupation.note: He advertises as a clothier and grocer in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, self-reported at the EAST END OF SOUTH WATER-STREET.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT WHOSE ADVERTISEMENT DATES HIS ARRIVAL BACKWARDS. His copy addresses 'old customers' and thanks them for 'past favors', which is a man who had been trading in Chicago for some time before November 1833 - the only such statement in the issue. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Cohen, Peter” (poll_1834_026, line 195); Poll list of 1835 — “Cohen, Peter” (poll_1835_016, line 301). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Cohen' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: ONE OF THE SIX DEMOCRAT ADVERTISERS THIS PARCEL CAN GIVE A SELF-REPORTED ADDRESS. Cohen, W. Kimball, Goss & Cobb and Matthias Mason & Co. all state where they are; Philo Carpenter, C. & I. Harmon, B. Jones and Newberry & Dole do not. That split is worth carrying forward: an 1833 advertisement with a street in it is a placement constraint for a structure record, and one without is only a trade.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Cohen, Peter, merchant, South Water street'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
